newsitem.title: USA: Forces in place to balance U.S. budget, Rubin says.
newsitem.headline: Forces in place to balance U.S. budget, Rubin says.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin on Friday saw good chances for agreement on a plan to get rid of government red ink, but said a balanced budget amendment to the constitution was not the way to do it.

"Politically, historically and economically, the forces are in place to balance the budget," Rubin said in prepared statement to the Senate Judiciary Committee. "We are not far apart. Now we need to get the job done."
He argued that that the balanced budget amendment being pushed by Republican lawmakers would hurt, not help, the economy and was not necessary to end government red ink.

"A balanced budget amendment is a threat to our economic health, will expose our economy to unacceptable risks and should not be adopted,' Rubin said. "It would seriously increase the risk of default on national debt," he added.

Passage of a balanced budget amendment requires a two-thirds vote by the House of Representatives and the Senate. It does not need presidential approval, but must ratified by three-quarters of the states.
The House two years ago approved a balanced budget amendment but it failed by one vote in the Senate.
Rubin laid out a series of reasons to reject a balanced budget amendment.
By tying the government's hands, it could turn economic slowdowns into recession and recessions into depressions.
Treasury estimates that the unemployment rate might have hit nine percent in 1992, instead of 7.7 percent, if a balanced budget amendement had been in place, Rubin said.
"As Secretary of Treasury, I am also highly concerned that limits on our flexibility would increase the risk of default on the federal debt," he added.

Rubin also argued that a balanced budget amendment might be unenforceable. "There is no way to compel Congress and the President to enact legislation to cut spending or raise taxes to balance the budget," he said.

In explaining his optimism that the budget can be balanced without such an amendement, Rubin said he believed that the "atmosphere in Washington has changed" after what he termed the "fiscal indiscipline" of the 1980's.
There are also factors at work in world financial markets pushing Washington to greater budget discipline, he said.
"A nation that does not address fiscal matters will be severely punished by markets with high interest rates that could impair or even severely impair its economy," Rubin said.
